title: Learning to clear a cluttered pile
summary: A MuJoCo + reinforcement-learning pipeline that decides which object a robot should remove next to reach a buried target, without collapsing the pile around it.

hero_media.alt: Diagram of the observe, decide, execute loop with the task module computing the reward
hero_media.caption: The loop the whole codebase is organized around. Each block has a typed contract, so perception, policy and robot can be swapped independently.

tldr: Built so far: procedural scene generation, physics diagnostics, simulated sensors with a trained segmentation detector, and a PPO training pipeline with a teacher–student design.
Measured so far: simple rule-based baselines; the learned policies have not been evaluated yet.
Planned: full training and ablation runs, then a simulated UR5 and transfer to the physical robot.
facts: Research intern — I develop this project independently and review it with my supervisor

sections.title: The problem
body: A target object lies somewhere inside a pile of other objects. To reach it, a robot has to remove objects one at a time — but some of them hold others up. Remove the wrong one and the pile collapses onto, or around, the target.

Geometric contact alone doesn't tell you which object is actually supporting which, and the robot only sees the scene through cameras. The question is a sequence of decisions under uncertainty, which is why the core of the project is a learned policy rather than a fixed rule.

sections.title: Architecture and status
body: The code is organized as a loop: observe the scene, decide one object to act on, execute, then check what actually happened. Only the simulation layer talks to MuJoCo, and every experiment is defined by a config file rather than by branches in the code.

list: Observe — implemented: simulated stereo, RGB-D and LiDAR sensors with calibration, a segmentation detector trained on domain-randomized synthetic images, and a privileged ‘oracle’ observer that reads the support graph from MuJoCo contact forces. The decision module currently runs on the oracle observation; switching it to the sensor pipeline is planned.

Decide — implemented, not yet evaluated: one object per step, trained with PPO. The design is teacher–student: a teacher learns on the true simulator state, and a student that receives only the observation imitates it and then keeps improving. A geometric check rejects objects the gripper cannot reach from any side.
Task — implemented: the reward is split into named terms (progress, disturbance of the target, objects falling near it, refused actions), and episodes end on critical events.
Execute — implemented as an abstract removal that returns the verified outcome; a simulated UR5 arm will replace it.

sections.title: Checking the simulation
body: Before trusting any learning result I made sure the simulator measures what the task needs. Two examples:

list: Scenes were settled for a fixed 0.4 s. With ten objects the release height reached 1.3 m, and a 1.3 m drop takes about 0.5 s — so reference poses were recorded while objects were still falling, and every ‘disturbance’ was really fall distance. I replaced it with settling until the scene is at rest.

With the default rolling friction, cylinders landing on an edge rolled away by about 25 cm and the target ended up buried in 0 of 10 test scenes. Raising rolling friction from 0.005 to 0.05 produced buried targets in 6 of 10. This is a configuration choice that makes the scene distribution match the task; it does not show the physics is more realistic, and the friction parameters will be calibrated against real objects before any sim-to-real claim.

body: Reproducibility check: for the same seed, on the same machine and software versions, the generated scenes are byte-identical; a regression test over 60 episodes compares scene and episode records before and after each refactor (timing fields excluded).

list: A persistent bank of pre-settled scenes with an 80/20 train/evaluation split, so training doesn't spend its time waiting for piles to settle.
16 asynchronous MuJoCo workers, with a guard that refuses to start if any worker loaded a different configuration.

Resumable training: a checkpoint restores weights, optimizer state, schedules and random-generator states, verified with checksums. Because workers are asynchronous, a resumed run is not guaranteed to follow the exact same trajectory as an uninterrupted one.
An ablation benchmark, ready to run, that compares the learned decision-makers against rule-based baselines on the same scenes.

sections.title: Results so far
body: Measured so far are only simple rule-based baselines. On 25 episodes with 6 objects, always removing the top object succeeded 24/25 times, a random choice 21/25, and going straight for the target 18/25 — the order of removal matters.
The learned policies have not been evaluated yet. I'll publish the ablation results here once the first full round with three seeds is complete.

list: Add a simulated UR5 arm in MuJoCo: grasp selection, inverse kinematics, collision checking.
Bring learning into the execute module as well, so the arm's motions are a policy too — the design is still open.
Transfer from simulation to the physical UR5 and measure the gap.
Move from perfect state to stereo perception, with occlusion and uncertainty.
